To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the predictability and the spatiotemporality of the saccade task, despite not affecting attentional selection before movement preparation, largely improves the accuracy of short-latency saccades.

(1) the spatial predictability (and hence spatial uncertainty) of target and distracter locations during episodes of competition substantially improved the accuracy of saccades and (2) that this was associated with a selective enhancement of visual attentional resources to a saccade-target location only before saccades landed accurately at this location.

the accuracy of short-latency saccades was enhanced by the predictability of the saccade targets and distractors, and that this enhancement was related to a more selective deployment attentional resources to saccade targets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that underlie the control of eye movements in the presence of competing objects in the visual field.
the spatiotemporally selective deployment of attention during the preparation and execution of saccadic eye movements.
how the human brain selects and controls the eyes in order to process and respond to visual stimuli in our environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the predictability in target location and short go signal delay improved the accuracy of saccades and the deployment of visual sensitivity to the target.

our findings provide novel insights into the relationship between the deployment and dynamics of selective visual attention and the control of saccades in the presence of competing distractor objects.

the predictability in the spatiotemporality of the saccade task (i.e., the spatial predictability and the short go signal delay) improved saccade accuracy and enhanced visual attentional selectivity, which was associated to an improved visual discrimination performance at the saccadic target.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the deployment of attentional and motor resources is highly flexible and adaptive to the spatiotemporally varying task demands.

saccade target predictability, as well as a short go signal delays, improve saccade accuracy and the spatial distribution of visual attention, which in turn enhances visual discrimination performance at the saccadic target location.
the spatio-temporal deployment of visual attention is a key factor in the successful selection of saccade target locations during oculomotors competition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
saccade target location is not only selected during movement preparation but also selected during saccade execution.
the deployment of attentional and motor resources is tightly linked and that this link can be exploited to improve the efficiency of saccade control during oculo-motor competition.

top-down oculomotor control is largely independent of the spatial predictability and temporal dynamics of visual attention, but that it relies on the capacity to selectively allocate visual attentional resources to saccade target locations during movement preparation.
